set.approach: Drive to the Pacific Crest Trail trailhead near Big Lake, reached by the Santiam Wagon Road, which branches off the Big Lake road just before the lake. Hike the PCT for about 3.5 miles; at a junction a climbers' trail heads left (east) and leads to treeline and the defined north ridge. From there the path winds on to the upper rock pinnacles and the notch below the summit block, where most parties rope up.
set.descent_text: Descend by rappelling from the fixed stations on the upper pitches, with a 50 or 60 meter rope depending on the stations used. Below the first pitch the terrain eases to scree, which can be glissaded, to a descent trail through meadows that rejoins the PCT. Allow roughly three to four and a half hours from the summit back to the trailhead.
hazards: Friable volcanic rock with unreliable protection; a leader fall would be serious
Loose gully before the final pinnacle
Ice and rime on the upper rock, which makes holds wet and slick
Wet downclimbing at the second-pitch step after ice melts

review.notes: Rappel count left out: one page says three, the other says the first pitch only. Season from trip reports July to October.

set.overview: The standard route up Mount Thielsen, a jagged volcanic spire east of Diamond Lake that is nicknamed the Lightning Rod of the Cascades. A maintained trail leads to the Pacific Crest Trail, then the West Ridge climbs scree to the base of the summit horn. The last roughly 80 ft is an exposed scramble, usually fourth class with a few low fifth-class moves, and many climbers bring a rope. The round trip is about 9 miles with roughly 3,300 ft of gain.
set.approach: Park at the Mt. Thielsen trailhead beside Highway 138 just east of Diamond Lake; a Northwest Forest Pass is required. Follow trail 1456 up gentle switchbacks for 3.5 to 4 miles to the Pacific Crest Trail. Cross it and climb a rocky social path up the West Ridge, then a tiring, shadeless scree slope, to reach the foot of the summit horn about 4.5 miles from the car.
set.descent_text: Reverse the route: downclimb the short summit scramble, then descend the scree slopes of the West Ridge to the Pacific Crest Trail and follow trail 1456 back to the trailhead. In snow the upper slopes can be skied or snowshoed, but the final pinnacle itself usually needs downclimbing.
hazards: Lightning: the summit horn is among the most-struck points in the Cascades
Exposed final pitch with drops of 1,000 ft or more; avoid it when icy or snowy
Loose, unstable scree below the summit horn and crumbling rock above
No shade or water on the upper route

review.notes: Season window inferred: one page recommends early summer, trip reports run to early October. One page says 5 miles round trip; two others and the row waypoint say about 9, so I used 9. Class of the last pitch varies (4 to 5.1) by source.

set.approach: Park at the St. Huberts lot on Route 73 in Keene Valley, opposite the Roaring Brook Falls trailhead, with an Adirondack Mountain Reserve parking reservation in hand; one is needed for every visitor from May 1 to October 31, walkers included. Follow the road about half a mile, turn left onto Lake Road Way to the entrance station and gate, then walk roughly 2.5 miles of dirt road to the foot trail for Elk Pass. The summit lies about 1.7 miles of steep climbing past the beaver ponds.
set.descent_text: The usual way down makes this a loop over Dial. From the summit, return to the junction a tenth of a mile below, then continue about 2.1 miles along the ridge to the top of Dial. From there the Leach Trail drops about 3.8 miles to Lake Road, and the gate and parking lot are a further stretch of dirt road and pavement beyond.
hazards: Steep, sustained climbing for the last 1.7 miles, and the descent over Dial is also long and steep
Long day on a private-land approach: a parking reservation is required May 1 to October 31 and dogs are not allowed
Winter ascents need snowshoes and traction, and the summit can run 20 F colder than the trailhead

review.notes: Gain, distance: both published figures (13 mi, 4,300-4,388 ft) are for the whole Nippletop-Dial loop, not trailhead to summit, so skipped. Season: no page states a window (hikeable year round), skipped.

set.overview: The Santanoni Express is the direct herd path to the summit of Santanoni Peak, one of the highest and most remote of the Adirondack 46. A gravel road and a marked trail carry you to a cairn near some cascades, and from there an unmarked path crosses Santanoni Brook and climbs steeply, finally very steeply over eroded ground, to the ridge just north of the summit. It is a strenuous Class 2 day with route-finding and no maintained tread above the cairn.
set.approach: Start at the Santanoni Road trailhead near the Upper Works parking area outside Newcomb. Walk the old gravel road for 1.8 miles, then bear sharply right onto the foot trail, which crosses several footbridges. Continue to a brook with cascades, about 3.4 miles from the car; a cairn at the end of a flat section on the left marks the start of the Express herd path. The path crosses Santanoni Brook early, then climbs to a T on the ridge, where left leads a tenth of a mile to the summit.
set.descent_text: Retrace the herd path from the ridge T down to the cairn, then follow the marked trail and the gravel road back to the trailhead. The upper section is steep and eroded, so descend carefully, and recross Santanoni Brook with care if it has risen. Parties combining peaks can instead go right at the T toward Times Square and Panther Peak and drop to the Bradley Pond trail.
hazards: Very steep, eroded and loose footing on the herd path above the cairn
Santanoni Brook crossing can be hard in wet weather or at the start and end of winter
Easy-to-miss turnoffs: unmarked above the cairn, so a map and compass are needed
Slippery, high footbridges on the lower trail and no cell service

evidence.fact: 2,860 ft total gain, summit 4,607 ft
9.6 mi round trip; 4.8 mi one way = 7.72 km

review.notes: Gain and distance are one source only (other pages give range-loop figures). Season skipped: no page states a window.

set.overview: Panther Peak is climbed by the Panther Brook herd path, an unmarked track that leaves the Bradley Pond trail at a cairn. It runs mostly flat past Bradley Pond and steepens, then dips briefly to Panther Brook, which it follows up to the ridge. The summit is a short walk to the right. It is a Class 2 day, often paired with Santanoni, with muddy ground and a swampy stretch near the top.
set.approach: Start at the Santanoni Road trailhead near Upper Works, Newcomb. Walk the gravel road 1.8 miles, then bear sharply right onto the marked foot trail and cross Santanoni Brook on a footbridge. Pass the Santanoni turnoff and continue to a cairn about 4.3 miles from the start that marks the Panther Brook herd path. Follow it past Bradley Pond, up to the ridge junction, and turn right for the final 0.4 mile to the summit.
set.descent_text: Go back down the herd path to the ridge-side brook, past Bradley Pond to the cairn, then follow the marked trail and the gravel road to the trailhead. Parties linking Santanoni can instead go left at the ridge junction toward Times Square and drop down the Santanoni side, though that needs a separate plan for the return.
hazards: No maintained trail beyond the cairn; turnoffs are easy to miss
Muddy sections and a swamp near the top where logs serve as crossings
Remote with no reliable cell coverage, and weather changes quickly

evidence.fact: 12.5 mi round trip
12.0 mi round trip

review.notes: Distance 12.25 mi mean halved = 6.125 mi = 9.86 km. Gain skipped: sources give 3,762 ft and 3,300 ft (over 10% apart). Season skipped. The Santanoni-link sentence in the descent is thin; trim if the reviewer prefers.

set.approach: Park at the Elk Lake trailhead near the end of Elk Lake Road, reached from Blue Ridge Road off I-87 exit 29. Take the Elk Lake-Dix trail about 2.3 miles to Slide Brook, then follow the brook for just over a mile to the base of the slide on the right. Climb the slide, then follow a ridge path about 0.3 mile to the summit. The first stretch crosses private land; the gate closes seasonally, and the trail closes in hunting season, adding about 4.6 miles round trip if you must leave the car at the Upper Elk Lake Road lot instead.
set.descent_text: Return down the ridge path to the top of the slide and descend the slide itself, taking care on its loose rock and dirt, then follow Slide Brook back to the Elk Lake-Dix trail and out to the trailhead. The route is out and back with no separate descent line.
hazards: Macomb slide is steep with loose rock, rubble and sand, and its upper exit is difficult
No maintained trail above the slide: map and compass skills are needed
Elk Lake Road gate and hunting-season closures can add several miles to the day
Weather changes quickly and help can be hours away

evidence.fact: 2,344 ft total gain
751 m (about 2,460 ft) gain
8 mi round trip
12.2 km round trip

review.notes: Distance: mean 7.8 mi round trip halved = 3.9 mi = 6.28 km. Gain uses the higher figure, which is consistent with the trailhead near 2,000 ft. Season skipped.

set.overview: Armstrong Mountain is reached from the Lake Road side by the Gothics access trail and the Beaver Meadow Falls trail up to the Great Range Trail. Ladders beside the falls and steep sections make the climb demanding, though the route stays on marked trail. From the junction, a short dip into a col and a final climb lead to a broad rock platform summit. A walk through private Adirondack Mountain Reserve land begins the day.
set.approach: Park at the St. Huberts lot on Route 73, with an Adirondack Mountain Reserve reservation if hiking between May 1 and October 31. Follow the dirt road to the paved road by the golf course, turn left at about half a mile between the tennis courts on Lake Road Way, and continue to the reserve gate. Walk the dirt road for about 2 miles to the right-hand Gothics access trail, cross the Ausable River bridge, and reach the base of Beaver Meadow Falls. Climb beside the falls to the Great Range Trail and turn right for Armstrong.
set.descent_text: Go back along the Great Range Trail to the junction near the top of Beaver Meadow Falls, then descend the steep trail and ladders beside the falls to the Gothics access trail and the Lake Road. The same route leads back along the dirt road to the lot. The drop into the col below the summit is steep in both directions.
hazards: Slippery rock and a ladder beside Beaver Meadow Falls, plus further ladders and steep ledges
Steep drop into the col before the final climb to the summit
Reservation required May 1 to October 31 on reserve land, and dogs are prohibited
Winter ascents need snowshoes and spikes or crampons

evidence.fact: 3,500 ft gain, Beaver Meadow Falls out and back
11.2 mi round trip halved = 5.6 mi = 9.01 km

review.notes: Second source for this line not found (the other page describes the Upper Wolfjaw approach). Season skipped.

set.overview: South Dix, also known as Carson Peak, is the first summit past Macomb on the Dix Range crest, reached by an unmarked, unblazed herd path. The path crosses the summit area, drops steeply, then climbs over a broad sweep of bare rock. It is a long, strenuous day in the wilderness with no maintained trail beyond the Macomb turnoff.
set.approach: Start at the Elk Lake trailhead at the end of Elk Lake Road. The last stretch of road is closed to cars, so parking is at Clear Pond, which adds about 2 miles each way on foot. A marked trail leads to the lean-to and campsites at Slide Brook, where the Macomb herd path begins. Cross the brook, climb the steep loose slide to Macomb, then follow the crest path onward to South Dix.
set.descent_text: Retrace the herd path back over Macomb and down its slide to the marked trail, then walk out to Elk Lake and the road. Parties who continue along the range to Hough and Dix usually come down the marked Beckhorn Trail instead, which is steeper but shorter than the Hunter's Pass option.
hazards: Unmarked herd path that needs map and compass navigation
Steep, loose rock and scree on the Macomb slide
Steep drop and bare-rock climb near the summit area
Long day with a road walk at each end; high ground can run 20 degrees colder than the trailhead

review.notes: Gain and distance skipped: the only figures found are for the whole five-peak loop (15 mi, 5,350 ft), not this line. Season skipped: no page gives a window.

set.overview: Porter is reached by a short spur from the popular Cascade Mountain trail, off Route 73 near Cascade Lakes. The trail dips to the register, stays moderate, then climbs steeply over rocky ground and slabs. The summit is a large open rock with views of the Great Range and back to Cascade, and it is one of the easier High Peaks.
set.approach: Park along Route 73 toward Keene on the right before the Cascade Lakes. In summer the lot fills early and a road walk of a few hundred yards may be needed. The trail drops to the register, then climbs about 2 miles to a junction. Turn right there and follow the spur roughly 0.7 miles to the summit rock.
set.descent_text: Return along the spur to the junction and then down the Cascade trail to the highway. It is the same trail in both directions, so the way down is mostly steep rock slabs followed by easy ground.
hazards: Steep rock slabs that are slick when wet or icy
Very busy trail and crowded roadside parking in summer
Winter needs snowshoes and snow spikes on the slabs; summit can be 20 degrees colder than the trailhead

evidence.fact: 2.7 mi one way (5 mi round trip) = 4.35 km

review.notes: One-way distance is derived from the stated junction and spur lengths; a second page gives 6.2 mi round trip only for Cascade plus Porter, so no agreement. Season skipped. Gain already stored (1960); page lists 2,235 for the same line, left alone as gain was not in fill.

set.overview: Dial is reached from the St. Huberts side by a long walk on Lake Road and a rolling trail over Bear Den Mountain, which crosses the site of a 1999 forest fire. The summit is a large boulder that looks out toward the Great Range. It is a long, steep day on private reserve land.
set.approach: Park on Route 73 across from the Roaring Brook Falls trailhead. Walk 0.5 miles to a left turn between the tennis courts onto Lake Road Way and register at the entrance station. Pass the wooden gate and follow the dirt road for 2.5 miles to the foot trail. The Bear Den trail rises and falls for about 3.6 miles from Lake Road to the summit of Dial.
set.descent_text: Return over Bear Den Mountain on the same trail to Lake Road, then walk the road back to the parking area. Others loop it by going up Elk Pass and Nippletop and coming down this way.
hazards: Long road walk with an AMR reservation required May 1 to October 31
Rolling ridge adds extra climbing on the way back
Steep pitches on Elk Pass side icy in winter; snow spikes or crampons advised

review.notes: Gain and distance skipped: the page's 13 mi / 4,300 ft is the Elk Pass loop through Nippletop, not the Bear Den line. Season skipped.

set.overview: Grace Peak, formerly East Dix, is a pointed rock summit with nearly full views, reached by unmarked herd path heading roughly east from Carson Peak. It sits slightly off the main Dix Range circuit and is usually added to a long day over Macomb and South Dix.
set.approach: Begin at the Elk Lake trailhead; the road is closed short of it, so you park at Clear Pond and walk about 2 miles in. Follow the marked path to the Slide Brook lean-to and campsites, cross the brook and climb the steep Macomb slide. Continue along the herd path over South Dix, then head straight east to the Grace summit.
set.descent_text: Return west along the herd path to South Dix and Macomb, then down the Macomb slide to the marked trail and out to Elk Lake. Longer parties may continue to Hough and Dix and descend the Beckhorn Trail.
hazards: Unmarked, unblazed herd path requiring navigation
Steep loose rock and scree on the Macomb slide
Tight paths and rock scrambling on the Dix Range crest
Very long day; high elevations can be 20 degrees colder than the start

review.notes: Gain and distance skipped: no opened page gives figures for this out-and-back. Season skipped.

set.approach: Drive to Talkeetna, then fly by ski plane to the west fork of the Tokositna Glacier, landing directly below the West Face with camp a short walk away. From camp, roughly an hour of navigating crevasses on the lower glacier leads to a bergschrund crossing and the Access Couloir. Allow a full eight-day trip from Anchorage with weather margin.
set.descent_text: The usual way down is the West Face Couloir, by a series of rappels and some downclimbing. Roughly a dozen v-thread anchors are used. At the bottom, head back to the basin above base camp and walk a short distance around large crevasses to reach camp.
hazards: Crevasses on the glacier and a bergschrund to cross at the base
Sustained 5.9 mixed pitches and an overhanging aid crack on the nose
Rapidly changing weather and snow conditions that dictate the schedule
No easy way off once on the ridge, so the descent must be planned ahead

review.notes: One guide-service page for approach and descent. Final sentence about reversing the Harvard Route is from search results (AAJ trip summaries) and not from an opened page; remove it if reviewers want strict page-only facts. Skipped gain, distance (not stated), season (not stated).

set.approach: Start where the Illecillewaet Campground road ends, about five kilometres west of Rogers Pass. The Sir Donald trail climbs into the Vaux Glacier basin and on to the Uto-Sir Donald Col, a gain of roughly 4,100 feet taking about two hours for a fit party. A backcountry camping permit is needed for the low bivouac site beside Vaux Creek or the high one at the col. Below the col, take care not to follow a spur trail to campsites by mistake. From the col the arete begins immediately.
set.descent_text: The standard descent follows a bolted rappel line down the northwest ridge, then drops onto the west face for several more stations, after which an easy scramble through scree and ledges leads to the Uto-Sir Donald Col. Walk the trail from the col back to the trailhead. Carry one 50 metre rope, check every anchor, and wait until other parties are clear below you to avoid knocking rock onto them.
hazards: Rockfall onto parties below during the descent, a leading cause of accidents
Mistakes at the rappel stations
Afternoon lightning and fast-changing weather on the exposed ridge
Steep icy snow on the slopes below the col early in the season
No water on the route above the low bivouac

review.notes: Two independent pages for approach and descent; rappel station counts differ (15 stations vs 4+6 rappels) so no count given. Season window is from 'ridge usually free of snow by mid-late July' plus a late August ascent; September not evidenced.

set.approach: Leave the car at a pullout on Moraine Lake Road a mile or two short of the Moraine Lake parking area, and follow the trail that climbs the grassy slope north of the road toward the foot of the ridge. The grass gives way to talus, then a third-class ridge, then several hundred feet of moderate scrambling to a broad shoulder. That shoulder sits at the base of the Big Step, where the roped climbing begins with two or three pitches of steep 5.6.
set.descent_text: Most parties continue over the summit and walk down the southwest ridge, the heavily used scramble route, which leads back to the Moraine Lake area. Carry boots and an axe for the corniced summit ridge and any snow on the way down, and allow time for the long walk out along the lake road or shuttle.
hazards: Grizzly activity in the Moraine Lake area can bring a minimum party size of four on the approach and descent trails; check current restrictions before leaving
Loose rock throughout, with protection that is awkward to place
Soft cornices and possible crevasses along the summit ridge, unstable on warm days
Snow on the ledge traverses and in the upper half of the right-hand gully early in the season

review.notes: Gain skipped: only a 5,000 ft figure (looks like route length) and a 1,000 m guide figure that disagree with each other and with the geometry; no one-way distance found. Season skipped: no route-specific window on any opened page. Descent is the scramble route as stated on the route page; the roads/shuttle wording is generic.

set.overview: The easiest route to the top of Devils Tower and the most popular line on it, about 500 feet over six pitches. It follows the Leaning Column and a series of cracks on the south side, with off-width and chimney moves, and finishes by crossing a broad meadow-like ledge near the top. The crux is the second pitch crack, where a big cam is useful, and the final jump traverse can be avoided by a short direct crack.
set.approach: Register at the visitor center, then take the paved Tower Trail around the base to the south side. Either turn up a faint trail and easy ramp to the foot of the Leaning Column, or continue along the trail to a clear path that reaches the base of the tower in about five minutes, climb an easy crack, and traverse left on fourth-class ground to the column.
set.descent_text: From the summit, walk back to the top of the direct finish crack and downclimb a few feet to the first rappel station, which drops into the meadow ledge near the jump traverse. Downclimb right to the bolts below, then make three more rappels down the Bowling Alley, which lies a few hundred feet to the right of the climb. All rappels need two ropes; rappel over the nose of each pillar rather than in the crack to avoid a stuck rope. Sign out at the visitor center afterward.
hazards: Loose rock on the flake crack pitch
Ropes jam if rappels run down the cracks instead of over the pillar noses
Heavy traffic on the route; start at first light or late afternoon if you are fast
Seasonal falcon closures on some faces, and a voluntary request to skip the tower in June

review.notes: Gain, distance, season skipped: a short walk-in (optional) and no season window stated. Rappel count (three after the first) is from one page, so it is written loosely in the descent.

set.overview: A long granite buttress of about 1,500 feet and eleven pitches on the south side of Mount Moran, reached by canoe across two lakes. The climbing is sustained crack work with a double pendulum and a long hand traverse high up, and a short aid section that has been freed at a much higher grade. The buttress ends in a bowl roughly a third of the way up the peak; continuing to the summit adds easier scrambling and an exposed 5.6 ridge.
hazards: Loose stone in the descent chutes, plus a loose corner on the fifth pitch
Strong, sustained wind on the upper buttress, which makes aid and traverses harder
Grizzly bears have been seen in Leigh Canyon on the approach
Snow and ice in the bowl and gullies, particularly in snowy years or early in the season, call for axe and crampons
Easy to get lost on the approach pitches, and no running water in the bowl above

review.notes: Gain, distance and season skipped: the route ends partway up the peak and no trailhead-to-top figures or season window were found.

set.approach: Park at a pullout on the valley loop road past Bridalveil Falls and find the climbers' trail. The approach is short and straightforward but steep, gaining about 800 feet on the way up to the base of the buttress.
set.descent_text: Two options. The rappel line is a dedicated route just left of the tenth belay, using a 60 m rope for short rappels of about 20 m; do not climb the eleventh pitch. The walk-off follows a cairned bootpath and the faint Kat Walk to the gully between Middle and Upper Cathedral, which needs several rappels or scrambling and is hard to follow in the dark.
hazards: Snow in the descent gully early in the season can make it the crux
Exposed third class slabs and ledges on the walk-off, with a steep drop at the gully end
Rappel anchors in the gully damaged by rockfall
Falcon closures in spring, and fire or smoke closures

review.notes: Gain skipped: only the 800 ft approach climb, not a summit gain. Distance and season not stated. Page numbering of pitches is inconsistent (9 vs 10/11).

set.overview: The most famous big wall in Yosemite, about 3,000 feet and 31 pitches up the middle of the southwest face of El Capitan. At 5.9 C2 it is the easiest full-length route on the wall, which is why it draws so many parties, but it is sustained and exposed. Much of the climbing is 5.10 or easier and many people climb it in four or five days.
set.approach: Cross the road from El Capitan Meadow and take one of the obvious trails to a clearing. Follow the worn path north and slightly west to the wall, then go up and left around its foot and traverse back right to a dirt ledge at the start of the first pitch. It takes only 10 to 15 minutes.
set.descent_text: The standard way down from the summit is the East Ledges, a mix of rappelling, downclimbing and talus scrambling that has caused injuries and a fatality; consider waiting for morning light. On the route itself you can rappel from any pitch, but route finding matters and parties have got lost on the standard rap line.
hazards: Leader falls from pulled gear are the most common incident
Weather and stranding over the four to five days that most parties spend on the wall
Falling objects, rope-cutting rockfall, pendulums and rappel errors
Runoff above the upper camps after rain or snowmelt
East Ledges descent, which has caused injuries

review.notes: Season skipped: fall and winter are popular but no window is stated.

set.approach: From the Molas trailhead the trail drops about 1,700 feet over roughly four miles to the Animas River and crosses a bridge. Climb along the Colorado Trail for about 1.5 miles to the beaver ponds, then follow the steep, well-worn trail about two miles up into Vestal Basin, where a few fallen trees lie between roughly 10,000 and 10,300 feet. Many parties camp in the basin and climb from there; the climbing starts at the base of the north face above the basin.
set.descent_text: Do not take the first trail leading off the summit; it is loose, with kitty-litter ledges and 15-foot Class 3 downclimbs. Instead, from the back of the subsummit, descend a loose gully that stays at Class 3 or easier, cross the rib to your right where cairns mark a gap in it, then reach the saddle trail and the moraines that lead back to the basin camp.
hazards: Loose scree and kitty litter on the wrong descent trail
Exposed Class 3 downclimbs off the summit
Easy fifth-class upper ridge with a steep slab that is best bypassed
Long approach with a 1,700-foot climb back out at the end of the day

review.notes: Approach and descent come from one detailed report of the route; the approach is written as facts of the trail, not as a report. Skipped season (no page stated one). Gain/distance not in fill.

set.overview: A Class 2 walk up the south slope of Clinton Peak in the Mosquito Range, starting from the Montgomery Reservoir road south of Hoosier Pass. The route crosses a basin of water, mud and willows, then climbs tundra and talus with little exposure and easy route-finding. It is often done with the neighboring McNamee and Traver, which are reached along the ridge.
set.approach: From Colorado 9 just south of Hoosier Pass, turn west on County Road 4 and follow it to the west end of Montgomery Reservoir, where passenger cars park near 10,970 feet. Past that point the road is a rough four-wheel-drive track with rock slabs, deep mud and water crossings, so it is usually walked. Follow the Middle Fork of the South Platte upstream toward Wheeler Lake, then go up into the basin below Clinton, McNamee and Traver, and climb the south slope from there.
set.descent_text: Return the way you came: come down the south slope into the basin, cross the central stream, and walk the track out past Wheeler Lake to the reservoir. Descending the ridge toward McNamee and Traver is the alternative if linking peaks.
hazards: Dense willows, water and mud on the road and in the basin
Loose talus and rubble on the slopes
Rough four-wheel-drive road with rock slabs and a steep step
Snow in the basin early in the season can call for an ice axe

review.notes: Source pages describe the Traver-McNamee-Clinton combination (about 10-12.8 mi, 3,200-3,300 ft), not the south slope alone, so distance left out. Skipped season. Descent for Clinton alone is inferred as retracing the climb.

set.overview: Jupiter Mountain is a remote Chicago Basin thirteener in the Weminuche, reached only by train or a very long backpack. The southwest slope is a steep Class 2+ climb over tundra, then loose talus to a west ridge and a false summit, with the true summit among rock towers that need a little routefinding and scrambling. Most parties camp in the basin and climb it with neighbouring peaks.
set.approach: Ride the narrow gauge train to Needleton Bridge at 8,235 feet, or backpack in from the highway. Cross the Animas River to its east side, walk south about 0.8 miles to the signed junction, and turn left along Needle Creek. Follow it about 6 miles to Chicago Basin near 11,000 feet. Take either Columbine Pass trail to a meadow near 11,680 feet, then a faint climbers' path east-northeast across tundra to the base of the steep southwest slope.
set.descent_text: Come down the way you went up: the climbers' path off the slope to the 11,680-foot meadow, then the Columbine Pass trail back to Chicago Basin. Retrace the Needle Creek trail and the Animas River trail to Needleton and the train.
hazards: Loose talus and rubble on the steep upper slopes
Monsoon thunderstorms that make the climb unsafe on summer afternoons
Routefinding and minor scrambling among the towers near the false summit
High water at the Animas River crossing early in the season
Heavy crowding and a campfire ban in Chicago Basin in summer

evidence.fact: about 17 mi round trip, 5,630 ft total from Needleton (2,800 to camp + 2,830 above)
about 17 mi round trip; 8.5 mi one way = 13.68 km

review.notes: Single source. Season skipped (page gives only crowding and ford timing, no window). Train boarding rules changed in 2021; approach says 'or backpack' to stay safe.

set.approach: Park at the climbers' campground on Castle Valley Road and take the Castleton Tower trail up the wash and the steep talus cone. Near the top of the cone, a trail crosses over the ridgeline and runs to the foot of the Rectory. The Empirical Route is the far-left line on the west face, in the right-facing corner that separates the Rectory from the Nuns. Allow about an hour for the approach, which is strenuous; stay on the trail.
hazards: Third pitch is on rotten Wingate sandstone
Run-out sections carry an R rating
Wet sandstone is weak: do not climb in or just after rain
Summer heat and spring raptor closures in the area

review.notes: Descent skipped: no opened page describes it (a trip report mentioned two-rope raps but was only seen in a search summary). Gain/distance skipped (desert tower, optional, no summit figure).

set.approach: About 7 miles east of Moab on River Road, park at a small pullout on the river side, just past a large boulder with calcite on one side. Walk back toward Moab on the road to a trail marked by a metal post; the walk takes about 20 minutes to the west face. The route is on the east side, so first climb a short 5.7 approach pitch up a loose corner to a belay anchor in the south-side notch, then walk along the base of the northeast face to the chalked chimney.
set.descent_text: No anchors exist on the summit, so reverse the mantle onto the summit block and downclimb to the fixed anchors. Then either rappel the route with two ropes, walk to the approach-pitch anchors and rappel to your packs, or use a single 70 m rope down the northeast side, a short rappel to a ledge and a long one to the back of the spire.
hazards: Approach pitch is run-out and loose
No summit anchor; the overhanging summit block must be mantled and reversed
Wet sandstone is weak: do not climb in or just after rain
Heat in summer and spring raptor closures

review.notes: Gain/distance skipped. Rappel counts left out.

set.approach: Park at the end of the Fisher Towers road and walk the well-marked main trail for about a mile, past the tower. Turn left onto a climber's trail and follow it, watching for cairns, through the gully that lies between Ancient Art and Cottontail Tower to the base. The route starts with the same approach as Stolen Chimney, then walks about 200 feet right to a sandy slope.
set.descent_text: Walk back to the ledge at the end of the third pitch and rappel twice to a bench. From there either rappel again from a tree or downclimb the start of Stolen Chimney. There are no anchors on the summit itself, so downclimb the final mantle first.
hazards: Last pitch has no fixed protection and ends on a mantle with no summit anchor
Mud-coated, loose Fisher Towers sandstone
Wet sandstone is weak: do not climb in or just after rain
Summer heat and spring raptor closures
set.overview: A four-pitch trad and aid line up the north summit of Ancient Art in the Fisher Towers, sharing its first moves with Stolen Chimney. It follows an arch (5.8), a 5.10+ chimney to a big ledge, a 5.8 offwidth squeeze, and a final unprotected mantle to the top. The sandstone is soft and mud-coated, protection is sparse near the top, and a 70 m rope is suggested.

review.notes: Gain/distance skipped (optional). Season line is the Moab-wide spring/fall summary from a guide page about Castleton, not Fisher Towers specific.

set.approach: Park at the end of the Fisher Towers road and hike the main trail, roughly 40 minutes to the Kingfisher area. Leave the trail and scramble steeply up loose ground toward the base, passing Ancient Art and the Cobra tower. The line begins about 50 feet to the right of Dead Again.
set.descent_text: Rappel the route. A single-rope rappel reaches the pitch 4 anchors, then double-rope rappels reach the ground. All the bolts have hangers and the pulls are easy.
hazards: Hard aid on the first and second pitches; falls on thin placements are likely
Mud-coated, loose sandstone and rockfall, especially from parties above
Wet sandstone is weak: do not climb in or just after rain
Summer heat and spring raptor closures
set.overview: A five-pitch, 600-foot aid route on the Kingfisher in the Fisher Towers, rated A3 overall. About 50 feet right of Dead Again it begins with a long first pitch of about 170 feet, then links thin crack systems with a couple of bolts, followed by A2 cracks, caprock and a short crack to the summit. It is a nailing-style line best suited to experienced aid climbers.

review.notes: Approach is from a trip report of another Kingfisher route (Northeast Ridge) -- the approach to the tower, not this wall. Gain/distance skipped. Season line is a Moab-wide summary.

set.approach: Drive the signed Davis Canyon road, which turns to high-clearance four-wheel-drive track within a short distance, and park where a track bends toward the foot of the talus cone; the tower stands west of the road. Do not take the southern line that heads into scrambling over the white rim. Head instead for a gap in the rim further north, follow the rim along until you are below the east face, and finish up a passable trail over the last hump. Liquid Sky and the neighbouring roof crack are visible above as you arrive.
set.descent_text: From the summit, rappel south into the chimney and notch above the big roof, where an old bolt ladder sits; inspect it before trusting it. From the notch, rappel on three bolts of doubtful quality along the formation's west side to the ground, so back up or replace worn anchors if you can.
hazards: Squeeze chimney through a roof that is strongly dependent on body size and can stop a larger climber
Rappel bolts on the west side of the tower and the old bolt ladder in the notch are of doubtful quality
Long sections of offwidth and squeeze climbing that are strenuous and awkward to protect
Sandstone is fragile when wet and holds can break, so avoid climbing during or just after rain

review.notes: Season, gain, distance skipped: no page opened states them. Descent is the tower's normal descent as the area page describes it, not specific to this line.

set.approach: Continue past the Bridger Jack mesa and the two Sixshooter towers, then turn left onto the signed road into Davis Canyon. Several miles up this road, which needs high clearance, leave the vehicle in the dry creekbed at the easiest spot on the mesa where the road starts to leave it. A cairned trail climbs the mesa and keeps you off the fragile crust of soil; allow roughly an hour of steady uphill walking to reach the base of the tower.
hazards: The road up Davis Canyon needs high clearance and gets rough, so a vehicle can be stranded far from help
Sandstone breaks easily when wet, so avoid climbing during or after rain
Long uphill walk-in with no facilities, so carry water and pack out waste
set.overview: A three-pitch trad line up the south side of the southern of the two Sixshooter sandstone towers near Indian Creek, in the Davis Canyon area. It is graded 5.7 with a point of aid noted, which makes it one of the more moderate ways onto a desert tower. The real effort is the long uphill walk to the base, and the summit gives a wide view over the canyon country.

review.notes: Descent skipped: the pages opened had none (other pages only seen as search summaries; they suggest a rappel of the face, not verified). Season, gain, distance skipped. Grade 5.7 is as the database holds it; some other listings call the normal line 5.6.

set.approach: Reach Taylor Canyon in Canyonlands National Park by the Mineral Bottom road and the steep descent to the Green River, then drive about five sandy miles up the canyon to the campsite. From the parking area just beyond the campsite, follow the obvious cairned trail that climbs the talus cone and reaches the tower's base. The walk is roughly a mile out and back, about an hour, with some 700 feet of climbing. Without a permit or high clearance you must instead hike down the Alcove Spring trail, which turns this into a very long day.
set.descent_text: Rappel the north face on short double-rope rappels, using the fixed anchors; the older stations there have been replaced with double bolts joined by a chain, but check each before committing. The descent down the south side is not obvious, so most parties come down the north side and then retrace the trail to the parking area.
hazards: Friable sandstone and potentially poor belay stances typical of desert towers
Tunnel pitch is a dark tight squeeze that a larger-chested climber may not fit through
Crux corner widens to an overhanging offwidth that needs many large cams and is strenuous at the top
Warm walk-in and strong gusts; sand and dust make camping unpleasant
Road down to the river is steep and washes out in storms, so skip it if rain or snow is forecast

review.notes: Rappel count omitted: one page says five short double-rope raps, another says four; they disagree. Gain and distance skipped: the park trail figures (1.3 mi round trip, 717 ft change) are to the base only. Season skipped.

set.approach: Zeus stands in Taylor Canyon beyond Moses. Drive down to the end of the canyon road past the campsite, take the cairned trail up the talus cone to Moses's base, and keep walking up the trail past Moses to reach Zeus. The park trail is about a mile and a quarter out and back from the road.
set.descent_text: Rappel down the tower's northeast side, using the fixed anchors on the way down, and then walk back along the trail past Moses to the parking area. Two ropes are needed to reach the ground in the longest rappel.
hazards: Third pitch crux is poorly protected and a fall would land on the ledge below
Several pitches rely on old drilled pins and belay anchors of uneven quality
Sandstone is fragile when wet, so avoid climbing during or after rain
set.overview: A three-pitch, 250-foot trad route up the south face of Zeus, a sandstone tower in Taylor Canyon on the Island in the Sky. It follows a dihedral on the left side of the face, with a finger crack and drilled pins on the first pitch, a strenuous thin lieback crack on the second, and a poorly protected 5.11 crux on the third. The R rating is earned on that final pitch, where a fall would hit a ledge.

review.notes: Rappel stated as one long (about 200 ft) rappel by one page only; text says two ropes needed without a count. Approach reuses Moses parking since the Zeus page just says walk past Moses. Season, gain, distance skipped.

set.approach: Drive the Potash road to the Shafer and White Rim junction, then follow the White Rim road to a parking area on slickrock beneath the towers. Hike up the canyon until a trail leaves to the left toward the towers. From there either head for the Washer Woman and Monster Tower saddle, which needs some easy fifth-class climbing from steep talus on the south side, or contour around the base of Monster Tower to the west face where the route starts.
set.descent_text: Rappel the line of the Kor Route with two ropes. The first rappel returns to the base of the last pitch, onto its ledge, the second goes through the arch and hangs free down the face to bolted anchors, and with two 60 m ropes the third reaches the ground. Otherwise stop at one of the other sets of bolts to rappel again.
hazards: Loose rock on the first pitch and rotten bands on the final pitch, with a runout 5.9 section
Free-hanging rappel through the arch is exposed and getting over the edge is intimidating
Loose rock may be dislodged when pulling ropes on the second rappel
Sandy, sloping holds where the chimney on pitch two exits
Long drive on rough White Rim road and a scrambling approach to the saddle

review.notes: Rappel count stated as two to three by the page itself, so I described the sequence without a number. Season, gain, distance skipped.

set.approach: Park on the road southwest of the towers just before the wash where the road turns left, pulling as far off the road as you can. Head up the ridgeline just north of the parking, climb the benches to the final talus slope, then traverse from the south end of Monster Tower around to the east side, just below the notch between the towers, where the route begins.
set.descent_text: Rappel the route on single-rope rappels with a 70 m rope, using the fixed anchors found atop each pitch. Hang on to the line you climbed so the ropes do not snag on the ridge, and return down the approach path to the parking area.
hazards: Fourth pitch carries the most loose rock on the tower
Final pitch bulge and bolt ladder may need aid, with a summit that has no real anchor
Rangers warn against parking off the roadbed, so pull well clear
Sandstone is fragile when wet, so avoid climbing during or after rain

review.notes: Another page (not opened) describes a multi-rappel descent, so no rappel count given. Season, gain, distance skipped.

set.approach: From Highway 313 on the Island in the Sky, turn onto the Mineral Bottom road and follow it to the switchbacks down to the river. Turn left along the river for a couple of miles to the park boundary, then zero your odometer and go 1.2 miles beyond the boundary. The towers show on your left, up a wash, and you walk up that wash to the base of the needle.

review.notes: Descent, hazards, season skipped: the only pages mentioning them were search summaries or a database mirror that returned 404 when opened. Approach covers the drive and the wash only, not the final climb up to the base.

set.approach: Start at the end of the main road in Arches National Park, in the Devils Garden parking area. Follow the main trail to Landscape Arch, continue onto the Primitive Loop, and look for the signed spur just south of Double O Arch that leads to the spire. The approach is about two miles each way past several arches and needs moderate scrambling in places; stay on established trails and washes and off the fragile ground crust.

review.notes: Distance skipped: one page says about 2 miles, the other 4.9 round trip, which differ by more than 10%. Descent, hazards, season skipped: no opened page gives them for this route (rappel details only seen in search summaries).

set.approach: From the Arches visitor center drive 9.3 miles and turn right onto the Windows road. After 1.1 miles, the Garden of Eden parking area is on the left; Owl Rock is the spire to the east-southeast, only about 200 feet from the start. Use established trails and avoid the fragile ground crust, and reach the base by the west ramp rather than the crumbly steps on the north side.
set.descent_text: Downclimb about ten feet from the top to the anchor just below the summit and rappel the route. A single 60 m rope is long enough to reach the ground from this anchor.
hazards: Crumbly sandy steps along the ramp's north side carry a groundfall of about twenty feet
Busy tower, so groups may queue at the base on weekends
Sandstone is fragile when wet, so avoid climbing during or after rain
set.overview: A short, popular 5.8 trad crack that climbs the obvious west side of Owl Rock, a sandstone spire beside the Garden of Eden parking area in Arches National Park. It is quick to reach and quick to finish, with sustained crack climbing that suits hands and fingers well, and the summit is only a short downclimb from the anchor.

review.notes: Season skipped (one page says any season, summers hot; not a window). Gain and distance not needed for a 200 ft walk-in.

set.approach: Park at the lot where the Courthouse Wash trail begins, on its north end. Walk the trail a few minutes until you are level with Argon Tower, then follow intermittent climbers' trails around the north end of the tower. These lead past the lower part of the tower to a bench on its west side, ten to fifteen minutes from the lot.
set.descent_text: Rappel the west face from the top of the fourth pitch. Two 60 m ropes may reach the ground in one rappel, but be ready to stop at a midway anchor and rappel again if you cannot see the ground.
hazards: Sandy, soft rock; a placed cam can be hard to remove
Poorly protected and loose holds on the upper corner pitch
Finish relies on a bolt ladder that is climbed on aid
Sandstone is fragile when wet, so avoid climbing during or after rain

review.notes: Season, gain, distance skipped. Pitch count on the route page is five whereas the database overview says four; I avoided giving a count.

set.overview: A two-pitch 5.10 on Easter Island, one of the small sandstone towers on the ridge between Bridger Jack Mesa and the Butte in Indian Creek. The opening pitch is a moderate stretch of jamming, around 5.8, that leads to a traverse right around the nose. Above that the route turns to face climbing, which is unusual in a crack-dominated area. The tower was the last in its group to be climbed.
set.approach: Drive into Indian Creek, take the signed Beef Basin Road, ford the river and pass the cattle guard, then turn right at once and follow the dirt road until the serrated ridge of Bridger Jack rises directly overhead. A truck is preferred, though low cars have made it. A large cairn between two campsites marks the trail that climbs to the base of the towers; walk the base trail to Easter Island.
hazards: Sandstone is weak when wet, so skip it during and after rain
Seasonal raptor closures in spring; confirm current areas with the land manager before climbing
Few toilet facilities at the base, so pack out waste

review.notes: Descent skipped: only a photo caption shows a rappel, no anchor or rope details. Season, gain and distance skipped (no page states them). Approach is the Bridger Jacks area approach, not Easter Island specific.

set.approach: Drive into Indian Creek and turn left onto the signed Beef Basin Road, then ford the river, pass the cattle guard, turn right immediately, and follow the road to the point beneath the serrated ridge of Bridger Jack. A large cairn between two campsites marks the trail to the base of the towers. King of Pain is the tall twin-summited tower; the line starts on its south side below the notch beside Hummingbird Spire.
hazards: Loose rock around the notch on the second pitch
Stuck ropes are common on the east-face rappels
Sandstone is fragile when wet, so avoid climbing after rain
Spring raptor closures apply in the area; check current limits first

review.notes: Descent is assembled from the neighbouring Sacred Space and Vision Quest pages (same tower, the route joins Sacred Space at the notch), not from a page on Egg Drop Soup itself. Gain, distance, season skipped.

set.overview: A single 165-foot pitch up the southwest arete of Thumbelina, which is the leftmost of the detached towers in the Bridger Jack group. It begins in a wide crack, about 5.6, then follows a bolted arete with face moves that feel more like gym climbing than Indian Creek splitters. There are several rests and some bouldery sections, a lower crux around 10+/11-, and a harder upper crux at the last two bolts before a mantle onto the summit.
set.approach: Drive into Indian Creek, take the signed Beef Basin Road, ford the river and pass the cattle guard, then turn right and follow the dirt road to the foot of the serrated Bridger Jack ridge. Take the obvious trail along the base of the cliff all the way to the left end, where the route starts in the wide crack leading to the left arete. A 50 m rope may need you to belay right at its base.
set.descent_text: Rappel from the summit with a double-rope setup. The tower is a short detached spire, so the rappel goes straight to the ground at its base; walk back along the base trail to the car.
hazards: Desperate moves at the last two bolts for many climbers
Sandstone is damaged easily when wet; avoid it after rain
Raptor closures in spring; verify with the land manager
Summit mantle exits onto a small top, so commit carefully

review.notes: Season, gain, distance skipped. The sentence about rappelling straight to the ground is an inference from the single 165 ft route length; the page only says double-rope rappel. Trim if the reviewer dislikes it.

set.approach: From the Castleton and Rectory trail junction in Castle Valley, walk along the Rectory's west side. For most routes you continue all the way around the Priest and come back a short distance to the base of the Nuns, about 15 minutes in total. The Nuns are the two short semi-detached towers at the north end of the Rectory.
hazards: Wet sandstone breaks and is permanently damaged; do not climb during or after rain
Spring raptor closures happen every year; check the current closure list before you go

review.notes: Descent, gain, distance and season skipped: no page opened states them for this route. Approach is the Nuns area approach.

set.overview: Angora Mountain is a remote summit above the Little Kern River in the Golden Trout Wilderness, rated class 2. The usual way follows trail to the Little Kern, then goes cross-country up Deep Creek and a ridge to a final stretch of boulders and talus. The challenge is the length of the approach and the brush rather than any technical ground.
set.approach: From the Lewis Camp trailhead, reached by Route 190, hike past Jerky Meadows and descend about 1,000 feet to the Little Kern River bridge. Leave the trail and go cross-country up to Deep Creek, bypassing a long switchback. Follow the creek, then cut through brush to the ridge running off the peak and follow it to the summit. The last few hundred feet are boulder-hopping and easy scrambling.
set.descent_text: Retrace the ridge and Deep Creek down to the Little Kern bridge, then climb the trail back out, roughly 4.5 miles and 1,800 feet to the trailhead. A ridge line down tends to be quicker than the creek bed.
hazards: Burn scar brush from the 2020 Castle Fire: thorny buckthorn, wild rose and sage
Trail overgrown or erased in places; carry a GPS track
Water is scarce; the reliable source is Deep Creek
Rattlesnakes and heat on a very long day

review.notes: Gain and distance skipped: both reports include other peaks or camping beyond the summit (30.8 mi combined loop; 19.16 mi day). Search-engine snippets of a one-way table not opened (SummitPost blocked). Season skipped.

set.approach: Start at the closed gate at the end of Mineral King Road and take the Franklin Pass trail as far as lower Franklin Lake, where there are bear boxes and campsites. Leave the trail before it switchbacks toward the pass and go cross-country toward upper Franklin Lake, skirting its high eastern shore toward the large cleft of the Great Chimney. The walk to the base is about 6.5 miles with roughly 4,000 feet of gain.
set.descent_text: Scramble class 2 and 3 ground down the northeast ridge, staying south of the crest, to sandy slopes and the trail at Franklin Pass. Return past the Franklin Lakes to Mineral King, about 8 miles from the summit to the trailhead.
hazards: Ledges carry debris and several large blocks are loose; keep the belayer out of the fall line
The loose chimney on pitch two is poor rock
Long approach and descent put the party far from the road

review.notes: Gain and distance skipped: the approach figure is to the base, not the summit, and no second source. Single published page for the approach and descent. Season skipped.

set.overview: Cartago Peak rises from the desert near the town of Cartago on the east side of the southern Sierra, and the standard climb is a steep, sandy slog of more than 6,000 feet in about five miles. The way is mostly class 2, up an old track, past two rock bands and onto a ridge. The true summit is the southernmost pinnacle at the southeast end of the summit plateau, finished with a few class 3 blocks.
set.approach: Turn off US 395 near the north end of Cartago onto an unsigned dirt road, cross the aqueduct and follow the aqueduct road south to a steep spur that ends at a wilderness boundary post near 4,000 feet. Parking at the post is tight; leaving the car on the aqueduct road adds about a quarter mile and 200 feet. Climb the wide old track and sandy slope to a first rock band, pass the second band, then reach the ridge near the saddle west of the 9,921-foot bump and continue to the plateau and the southeast pinnacle.
set.descent_text: A faster, gentler way down avoids the rock bands: from the large meadow east of the 9,921-foot bump, drop into the unnamed canyon that runs east to the aqueduct. It has little brush and easy sandy footing for plunge-stepping, and returns you to the car area in a few hours. Otherwise retrace the ascent and take care at the cliff bands.
hazards: Sandy slopes with poor footing and slipping for 2,000 feet or more
Two cliff bands low on the route with dense brush on the south side
Heat and swarming gnats on the lower desert face in spring
Snowbanks near 9,200 feet into late spring
Finding the true summit on the plateau, where several pinnacles look alike

evidence.fact: about 6,500 ft gain, about 4 mi one way
roughly 6,200 ft gain, about 10 mi round trip

review.notes: Distance skipped: 4 mi one way (1998) and about 5 mi one way (2006) differ by more than 10%. Assumed the standard route is the east-side Cartago Canal route; a PCT approach from Horseshoe Meadow also exists and was not used. Season skipped (reports are May and October, no window stated).

set.overview: Mount Newcomb is a 13,400-foot peak above the Crabtree Lakes on the Sierra crest, and its southwest slope is the easy side: sandy slopes and stable class 2 rock lead to the summit plateau. The ridge approach from Crabtree Pass is harder and slower, with class 3 sections. Most climbers take the Perrin Creek side or the Whitney Portal route over Discovery Pass.
set.approach: From the Whitney Portal side, climb the Whitney Trail past Trail Camp and the switchbacks, scramble over boulders to Discovery Pass, drop about 1,000 feet into the Crabtree drainage and climb to Crabtree Pass; the ridge from there is slower than it looks and reaches class 3. From the Cottonwood Lakes side, cross Old Army Pass to Rock Creek, find the obscure start of Perrin Creek, camp at the first lake of the upper basin, and cross a sand traverse to stable class 2 rock leading up to the plateau.
set.descent_text: Come down the southwest slope, an easy class 2 descent at a modest angle, or use the second-class chute on the east side that reaches the southwest corner of the summit plateau. From there return to Perrin Creek or Crabtree Pass and your approach route.
hazards: The ridge between Crabtree Pass and the summit is class 3 and costs far more time than the map suggests
Loose sand chutes on the upper slopes
Boulder field in lower Perrin Creek and a hard-to-find start
Perrin Creek holds little water until just below the lake basin; carry water

review.notes: Gain/distance skipped: pages opened give no figure for a single approach (Peakery loop figure of 25.5 mi is a different loop). Season skipped.

set.overview: Mount Kaweah is a 13,802-foot summit in Sequoia National Park, reached from Mineral King across two high passes and the Big Arroyo, then by a cross-country climb from the High Sierra Trail. The final slope is loose scree and talus to a saddle, then a rib and the summit ridge, where the first high point is a false summit and the true top is about a quarter mile beyond.
set.approach: Start at the Timber Gap trailhead at Mineral King and take the old use trail over Glacier Pass to Spring Lake, then Hands and Knees Pass and the Little Five Lakes basin. Descend to the Big Arroyo and the High Sierra Trail junction near 9,550 feet, then leave the trail and climb an off-trail rib to the Mount Kaweah and Second Kaweah saddle.
set.descent_text: Return along the summit ridge to the saddle, picking out sandy patches in the scree where possible, then drop to the High Sierra Trail at the Big Arroyo. Go back out by the same route over Hands and Knees Pass and Glacier Pass, which is a long climb on the return.
hazards: Loose scree and talus on the final slope below the summit ridge
Class 3 gullies on the Glacier Pass descent toward Spring Lake can cliff out in the dark
Steep granite slabs near Spring Lake force awkward sidehilling at lake level
Streams in the Big Arroyo can run very low late in the season

review.notes: One trip report only (30.1 mi round trip, user-logged); distance skipped because a personal GPS figure is not evidence and no second source. Season skipped (report written late fall, date unclear). Stored gain left alone.

set.overview: Kern Point is a 12,730-foot summit above the Kern-Kaweah drainage in Sequoia National Park. The standard line is a class 2 climb up granite slabs on the west-facing slope, reached from a camp after a long walk down the upper Kern, with a fairly long day on the peak itself.
set.approach: Start at the Shepherd Pass trailhead and hike down the upper Kern River to Junction Meadow, crossing the broad river near the meadow. Follow the Colby Pass trail, faint in many places, for about a half mile, then leave it and climb the granite slabs of the northwest slope toward the summit.
set.descent_text: Come down by a line slightly north of the one you went up; the paths on the slope are all much alike. Return to the Colby Pass trail and the camp in the Kern-Kaweah country, then walk out to Shepherd Pass trailhead.
hazards: Kern River crossing near Junction Meadow where the river spreads wide
Steep granite slabs on the way up and down are hard on feet and tendons
Faint trail along Colby Pass route and heavy mosquitoes at low camps in early summer

review.notes: One trip report; distance and season skipped. Report calls the slope northwest while the row says standard route; hedged. Stored gain 11,020 left alone.

set.overview: Triple Divide Peak is a 12,634-foot summit in Sequoia National Park where three watersheds meet. A party climbed it by the crest, up the west ridge and down the east ridge, in a long loop; the ridge is a hard class 3 with one or two class 4 moves, harder than its class 2 listing suggests.
set.approach: Start from Rowell Meadow, reached by a one-lane road off the Lodgepole road. Hike through Sugarloaf Meadow and along the Roaring River into Cloud Canyon, continuing to Glacier Lake. From the lake, climb toward the west ridge and follow its crest to the summit.
set.descent_text: Descend the east ridge, staying on or near the crest, and return to the Glacier Lake and Cloud Canyon trail. Another line, from Triple Divide Pass, stays on the face and climbs a last buttress.
hazards: The crest is a hard class 3 with one or two class 4 moves
Rockfall from the north face, including after small earthquakes
Long approach through Cloud Canyon makes it a multi-day trip

review.notes: One trip report (Aug 2003); describes a crest traverse, not necessarily the class 2 line the row lists. Gain, distance, season skipped, no figures. Row grade (Class 2) conflicts with the report's hard class 3.

set.overview: North Guard is a craggy, ridge-covered peak just north of Mount Brewer, and its west ridge, called the Parapet Ridge, is an easy fifth-class ridge climb along the crest. Granite talus leads to the crest from the southwest side, and the ridge ends at a long slab-like summit block that tilts over the steep east face. It is a long, off-trail objective well beyond the end of any maintained path.
set.approach: Start at Roads End in Cedar Grove and follow the Bubbs Creek trail east, crossing several small bridges and climbing switchbacks out of the canyon to the upper bridge. Turn onto the steep Sphinx Creek trail, then leave it at the creek crossing and work cross-country through wet meadows to Sphinx Lakes. Continue over Sphinx Col, drop toward the tarn near Echo Col, and enter the drainage between North Guard and Brewer. Climb talus on the southwest side to reach the west ridge crest.
set.descent_text: Come down the way you went up. From the summit block drop into a chute, then reach a narrow class 3 crack and ramp system, and traverse back across to the drainage between North Guard and Brewer before retracing the approach out to Roads End.
hazards: Rattlesnakes on the lower Bubbs Creek trail, from Junction Meadow to the Sphinx Creek crossing
Sphinx Creek trail has rough, loose blasted-granite tread that is hard on the feet
Cross-country route-finding at Sphinx Lakes and over Sphinx Col is slow and tricky in the dark
Steep, sloping summit block above the east face

review.notes: Approach and descent from one trip report plus MP page confirming Sphinx Trail and Sphinx Lakes. MP says approach to Sphinx Lakes is over 10 miles and ~5,500 ft but that is to the lakes only and single-source, so no dist or gain set. Season not found.

set.overview: Milestone Mountain is a 13,644-foot summit on the Great Western Divide, on the line where Sequoia and Kings Canyon national parks meet, about 0.6 miles south of Midway Mountain. Its name comes from the obelisk on its summit. The easiest route is an exposed class 3 scramble, first climbed in 1912, and it is a deep-backcountry peak that takes several days to reach.

review.notes: Wikipedia only; no approach, descent, distance, gain, season or hazard source opened. Skipped those.

set.overview: The North Arete is a six-pitch rock line up the northern crest of Matterhorn Peak, the high point of the Sawtooth Ridge above Twin Lakes. The pitches wander along a fractured, broken arete with mostly moderate climbing at 5.4 to 5.6, and the crux is a corner near the top of the route that is wider than it looks. A short exposed traverse around a gendarme leads to second-class ground and the summit. It is a long alpine day, and many of the moves feel stiffer than the 5.7 grade suggests.
set.approach: Start from the Twin Lakes trailhead near Bridgeport, where the Horse Creek trail leaves from behind the RV park. Switchbacks climb to meadows near 8,100 ft, after which the trail fades into brush and talus crossings. At a col around 9,500 ft, leave the main trail on a use trail up a ridge to a lake just above 9,800 ft. From the lake, follow a slabby ridge onto the moraine and cross a short, nearly level stretch of glacier, then climb the loose sandy gully to the start of the route, a fractured ramp about 200 ft below the prow of the arete.
set.descent_text: The usual way down is the southeast slope toward Horse Creek, which avoids the glacier and loose rock of the approach. Boot-ski the sand to the Matterhorn Peak and Twin Peaks saddle, then pick up the faint use trail down the drainage, which is easy to lose among talus and snow patches. Allow more time than the map suggests for this section, since the trail is often hard to follow.
hazards: Loose sand and rock in the upper approach gully
Loose scree above the third-pitch mantle
Exposed traverse around a gendarme on the summit ridge
Faint, hard-to-follow trail on the descent through talus and snow patches

review.notes: Single trip account for this line (late September). Season skipped: no stated window. Gain/distance not in fill.

set.approach: Start at the St. Marys Pass trailhead on the west side of Sonora Pass in the Stanislaus National Forest. The trail climbs through forest and then open tundra to the shoulder above St. Marys Pass. From there it runs mostly level for a couple of miles along the ridge until it ends at a cluster of white rock on Stanislaus Peak's east saddle. The climb up the south face begins at that saddle.
set.descent_text: Go back down the same way: descend the south face to the east saddle, then follow the ridge and trail to St. Marys Pass and the trailhead. Keep to the rim on the way down, since social trails branch off in many directions on the descent and can pull you onto loose slopes away from the main line.
hazards: Class 2 moves to get around the white rock at the saddle
Steep, loose social trail up the rim
Loose ground in the class 2 scrambling just below the summit
Many branching social trails on the descent

review.notes: Gain/distance skipped: the only figures found cover Stanislaus plus Sonora Peak. Season not stated.

set.overview: Highland Peak is the high point of the Carson-Iceberg area near Ebbetts Pass, with a lower south summit and a slightly higher north summit. This route follows the Pacific Crest Trail into Noble Canyon, passes Noble Lake, then takes a steep use trail to the saddle and climbs class 2 volcanic sand to the top. It is a long but non-technical day, with loose footing as the main complaint.
set.approach: Park in the day-use lot at Ebbetts Pass, which has pit toilets and a short spur to the Pacific Crest Trail. Follow the PCT south with switchbacks, dropping several hundred feet into Noble Canyon, and reach Noble Lake after about 4 miles. A use trail branches off the PCT where the lake's inlet is and climbs steeply to the saddle connecting with Highland Peak. From the saddle it is roughly another mile and a half to the lower south summit, with the higher north summit about three quarters of a mile beyond.
hazards: Loose volcanic sand on most of the summit climb and on the way down
Faint trail that can disappear in wet meadows or snow patches
Snow patches on the trail near Noble Lake early in the season

review.notes: Single report, distance is the author's estimate. Gain skipped: only 1,700 ft from the saddle stated. Descent skipped: the report came back a different way. Season not stated.

set.overview: Mokelumne Peak is the high point of the northern Mokelumne Wilderness, a rounded summit reached from the Tanglefoot trailhead by a trail and a short cross-country stretch. The route dips into Tanglefoot Canyon, leaves the trail in open forest, then climbs through brush to a saddle and follows an easy ridge to the top. It is class 2, and the main task is navigation through forest and manzanita.
set.approach: Reach the Tanglefoot trailhead by dirt roads from Bear River Reservoir; the roads are confusing and a GPS helps. Hike the trail through Tanglefoot Canyon, down one side and up the other, passing a small lake. Where the forest opens up, leave the trail, pass south of the bump at 8,628 ft, and head up to the saddle that joins that bump to Mokelumne Peak, working around the brush. A grassy watercourse is one way up to the saddle, and the ridge from there to the summit is easy.
hazards: Dense forest with few landmarks makes it hard to find where to leave the trail
Thick manzanita brush on the climb to the saddle
Little water: one spring on the climb out of Tanglefoot Canyon

evidence.fact: about 13 miles round trip; halved (6.5 mi)

review.notes: Assumes the row's standard route is the Tanglefoot line. Descent not stated; season not stated (late September and early August reports).

set.overview: An easy ridge-top walk on the Pacific Crest Trail to the summit of Tinker Knob, at about 8,950 feet. The trail runs at a gentle grade with one dip followed by a short climb, then switchbacks to a saddle, and a final quarter mile reaches the top. Views take in Lake Tahoe, Donner Lake and the canyon of the American River.
set.approach: Two ways reach the crest trail. From Olympic Valley, climb the Granite Chief Trail about 3.5 miles and 2,000 feet to the Pacific Crest Trail, then turn north along the crest about 3.5 miles toward the knob. A longer, easier approach comes along the crest trail from Donner Pass. Either way, the trail switchbacks up to the saddle just southeast of the peak, and a short final stretch of about a quarter mile leads to the summit.
set.descent_text: Walk back down the short summit spur to the saddle, then follow the Pacific Crest Trail the way you came, to Olympic Valley by the Granite Chief Trail or to Donner Pass, depending on where you started.

review.notes: One page. Hazards and season skipped: the page states none. Gain and distance were not in the fill list.
